summary:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a free, browser-based flight school where young learners train like real crews. It has six hands-on missions. In Launch Control, players make GO/NO-GO calls against written flight rules. In the Docking Simulator, they meet a station with limited fuel and no brakes. In Spacewalk Repair, they follow a repair card while suit oxygen counts down. In Life Support, they balance power between air, water and heat. In Gravity Lab, they compare one jump on six worlds. The last mission is a ten-question Mission Control Quiz.

Each mission has a briefing, a live simulation and a debrief. Players earn up to three stars per mission and rank up from Space Cadet to Mission Commander. The trainer answers the challenge by turning NASA’s real operations and planetary data into playable lessons about orbits, gravity, checklists and teamwork. It needs no install, works on laptops, tablets and phones, and saves progress only on the player’s own device.
details:
What it does
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a free, browser-based flight school for young learners. It has six replayable missions, each with a briefing, a live simulation and a debrief:

  1. Launch Control: make GO / NO-GO calls on eight console readings against written flight rules.
  2. Docking Simulator: fly a capsule to a station port with limited fuel, closing slower than 0.8 m/s.
  3. Spacewalk Repair: rewire three solar array panels from a repair card while suit oxygen counts down.
  4. Life Support: share 200 power units between oxygen, CO₂, water and heat for 60 seconds.
  5. Gravity Lab: jump beside an Earth twin on the Moon, Mars, Venus, Jupiter and Pluto.
  6. Mission Control Quiz: answer ten questions drawn from a bank of sixteen.

Players earn up to 3 stars per mission (18 in total) and rise from Space Cadet to Trainee, Flight Specialist, Mission Pilot and Mission Commander. Earning at least one star in every mission unlocks the Flight Certification.

How it works
The trainer is a single web page with no install. Each mission follows the same loop: Briefing, Train, Debrief, Stars, Rank. Quiz questions are reshuffled on every run, and the launch poll changes each time, so missions can be replayed. The Gravity Lab uses simple physics: every jump leaves the ground at 3 m/s, and height equals speed squared divided by twice the gravity. That gives about 0.46 m on Earth, 2.78 m on the Moon and 7.26 m on Pluto.

Benefits and intended impact
The trainer makes real astronaut skills approachable and free for young learners. It teaches that crews decide against written rules, that nothing in space slows down unless you thrust the other way, that spacewalks run on checklists, that supply must match demand in life support, and that gravity sets jump height and weight. We hope it builds curiosity and early STEM confidence, and that teachers and families can use it with nothing more than a browser.

Accessibility, privacy and design choices

  • It works on laptops, tablets and phones.
  • Players can use keyboard shortcuts, mouse clicks or an on-screen thruster pad for touch.
  • Wires use symbols as well as colors, sound can be muted, and reduced-motion settings are respected.
  • Progress is saved only in the player’s own browser, and nothing is sent anywhere.

We considered age-appropriate language, device flexibility, accessibility, privacy and replayability. We kept the physics simplified but accurate.

Tools and technology
HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript in a single file with no frameworks. It uses the Web Audio API for sound and browser local storage for saved progress. Typefaces are Big Shoulders Display, Hanken Grotesk and JetBrains Mono from Google Fonts. It was hosted as a static web page, and no special hardware is needed.

Creativity
Instead of a lecture, learners do the job. They make a hard call under time pressure, spend limited fuel, and watch the oxygen drain. Every mission ends with a debrief that explains why, so mistakes become lessons.

NASA data and resources
Gravity values come from the NASA Planetary Fact Sheet and Pluto Fact Sheet. Mission content draws on NASA spaceflight operations, such as GO/NO-GO polls and spacewalk (EVA) checklists, and on the Artemis Program.

Super Intelligence (SI) use
The code and text were created with assistance from Claude (Anthropic), a large language model, and reviewed by the team. This is stated in the project’s footer and page metadata.

Disclaimer
Independent student project, not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.
